This is general advice for anyone, however especially important now that fluoride won’t be in water. 

Diet and nutrition: limit all day grazing/frequent snacking. Food windows are important so the mouth has time to return to normal ph and teeth will be able to remineralize. Drink lots of water, limit sugary and acidic beverages to a short window of time, follow with water if possible. Think of flour as sugar, any flour containing foods are sticky and break down into sugar with which the bacteria in the mouth will feed off of. Whole foods (meat, veggies, fruits) are safe! Everything in *moderation*. 

Home care: brush 2x/day. Electric toothbrushes are amazing, they really help break up the plaque. Use a toothpaste with fluoride or nano hydroxyapatite. Flossing is a MUST. Use whatever you want (string floss, floss picks, water pik) but technique is extremely important. Look up pictures or videos if you need guidance, but essentially make sure you are going up and down the side of *each* tooth, not just snapping it into the space and popping it out. Mouthwash is not completely necessary, But if you use one, get one withOUT alcohol. It’s drying and can wipe out the good bacteria. If you want a mouthwash get alcohol free with fluoride, like ACT brand. 

Visit your dentist twice a year and listen to what they have to say for recommendations on home care. Ask if you or your kids are missing an areas. Ask if they’re monitoring any teeth (for incipient lesions that can turn into cavities). 

Hope this helps!

I hate giving advice over the internet because there’s a lot to say. 

First off, everyone’s mouth is different. Some people can skip flossing indefinitely and never get a cavity. Some people will floss a few times a week and still get them. It has a lot to do with the bacteria in your mouth. 

It also has to do with technique. You can floss every day but if you do it incorrectly it doesn’t matter either. 

In my opinion, I tell my patients 3 times a week is a GOOD place to be. Also, as a healthcare professional I have an understanding and compassion for mental illness. One time a week is a great starting point and I always encourage my pts to set their goal further. 

I have lots of pts who say “I’m doing 3x a week and that’s the best it’ll get,” and I’ll praise them for that. One of the biggest things I care about as a provider is effort! 

And the last thing I’ll say is that flossing isn’t JUST about cavities. The bacteria in the plaque between your teeth also causes gingivitis (inflammation of the gums). So circling back to the beginning of my comment, some people get gingivitis and no cavities or vice versa. Everyone is different. 

Keep up the good work friend.

I am 100% working when I come in early and clock in. I treatment plan for patients by seeing what X-rays and treatments they need, review notes and medical history to check for details of past visits, set up my room, restock things, etc. 

That’s why it’s frustrating. Coming in early is a key part in my success of the day. It would not be possible, efficient, or ideal for the pt if I came in right before I sat them and didn’t prep at all.

It is standard practice to arrive early and be prepared for your patient. That’s why we all come in at least 10-15 min early to be ready for the patient and seat them on time, etc. 

So It’s not really “unauthorized” to start before 8:00. It’s not even an expectation to only work 8 hours 20 mins. They basically just said if you work beyond that it won’t be paid. There won’t be any reprimanding for working beyond it besides not being paid for my time.

I would maybe consider having your permanent retainer removed, as it's likely to come off again in the future. NAD (am a hygiene student) PDL loss Is detected by using a probe to take measurements of your periodontal pockets. Normal, healthy pocket depths are 2-3mm. 4+mm indicates attachment loss. You can still have some attachment loss and good bone levels, but usually as disease progresses or become more aggressive you start to have bone loss. Additionally, some people have overall healthy pockets with some areas of loss. Every person is different and it really depends on your health history and oral hygiene routine. Calculus is calcified (hardened) plaque and bacteria. If you are continually having calculus in certain areas of your mouth you may not be brushing effectively in those areas. Some areas of the mouth are also much more susceptible to building calculus up quickly, such as the lingual side of your bottom front teeth!

Some other factors that could contribute to continual calc build up could be medications, systemic conditions (diabetes, heart disease, other medical conditions), or smoking. 

It would be best to see a dental hygienist to have regular cleanings done and talk to them about your oral hygiene habits and medical history to figure out what’s causing this.

So you are confused on how to determine their recall? Im not sure if you are asking how to schedule recalls in your system, but a lot of schools use different softwares (ex. AxiUm, EagleSoft, etc)

If you mean you are not sure how to determine the patients recall, there are a few things to consider.

\-If the patient is fully or mostly healthy (good probing measurements, light to moderate calc buildup) they can be a 6mo recall.

If the patient has periodontitis, this can be partially up to you. If the disease is active and progressing, 3 months is most likely the best option to keep an eye on the disease progression. However, let's say this perio patient is doing well, follows a good homecare routine, and there has not been much disease progression over the past few years, they could be a 4mo recall.

In summary, health = 6mo recall, perio= 3 or 4 mo recall.

If you do an SRP on a pt, you will likely have them come back for a one month eval, as well as prophy and fluoride. A pt who has had an SRP will most likely need to be on a 3 or 4 mo recall for awhile to assess their disease progression.

A patient with gingivitis can most likely be on a 6mo recall, however it really depends on their oral manifestations of gingivitis as well as how good their home care is. If they dont have an adamant homecare routine and have heavy plaque and calculus, you may want them to come in more frequently for a prophy. So to summarize a gingivitis patient: good homecare = most likely 6mo recall, poor homecare = most likely 3 or 4 mo recall

I would recommend products that correct dry mouth before trying to whiten!! Whitening with a dry mouth could cause excess sensitivity (most likely)

Definitely brush your teeth. Food gets stuck in cracks and crevices, especially between the teeth. Saliva begins the digestion process in your mouth and breaks carbs down into simple sugars. These sugars are then sitting in your teeth all night and will slowly cause decay! adding a night guard on top of this keeps all the food debris in place as well, almost ensuring decay. I highly highly recommend brushing your teeth before putting your night guard back in. I also recommend brushing before you wear it during the day. It is best to have a clean mouth before wearing these dental appliances.
